title: 5 Healthcare Staff Scheduling Options for Residency Programs
description: Healthcare staff scheduling for residency programs: Scheduling Wizard, spreadsheets, QGenda, Amion and Lightning Bolt, compared on ACGME requirements.
content:
Summary

  • Residency scheduling differs from general staff scheduling because of layered rules, the ACGME requirements, rotation sequences and call equity, that general-purpose tools are not built around.
  • It saves the most work when the rules go into the build rather than being checked after the fact. A study in Neurosurgery found a rebuilt call schedule reduced call variation by 70%, improving fairness.
  • The choice between self-service software and a managed service comes down to who does the scheduling. Self-service tools require a dedicated, permanent administrator, while managed services are built for rotating chief residents.
  • For programs relying on rotating chiefs, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard takes the build off their plate and delivers finished schedules built to the ACGME requirements the program tells us apply.

You just got handed the chief resident role. Congratulations: now rebuild the entire department schedule from scratch using the same Excel file your predecessor left behind, a file full of unlabeled formulas, color-coded cells no one can explain, and rotation logic that exists only in someone's head who just graduated.

Many new chiefs start this way. And it's why residency program forums are full of threads from chiefs venting that 'creating residency schedules in Excel is laborious and frustrating.' That's not because they're bad at their jobs, but because they've been handed a problem that general-purpose tools simply weren't built to solve.

Residency scheduling is a different problem from shift scheduling.

General healthcare staff scheduling software is built around filling open slots with available staff. Residency scheduling requires satisfying a layered system of rules simultaneously: ACGME Common Program Requirements on duty hours, block rotation sequencing, call equity across residents, clinic obligations, subspecialty-specific rules, and resident preferences, all while knowing the person managing all of this changes every single year.

Duty hour problems often show up as tired, unhappy residents before they show up anywhere else, and many programs still run on spreadsheets, manual checks and memory that leaves with each graduating class.

This guide breaks down five healthcare staff scheduling options for residency programs, including tools built specifically for GME and general platforms that programs commonly use, so you can find the right fit for your program's needs.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

One thing this list does not cover: nursing and hourly staff rostering is a different job with different tools, and we do not build those schedules. If that is what you need, a general workforce platform is a better place to start than anything here. This list is about physician and advanced practice provider schedules.

How to Evaluate Residency Scheduling Tools

Before the tools, three things to look at in a GME context. These three criteria separate tools that were built for residency programs from tools that were simply adapted to them.

1. Compliance Handling

Most tools in this space track ACGME duty hours in some form. The more useful question is when the rules come in: during the build, or after it.

Flagging after the build means the chief builds the schedule, the tool identifies problems, and the chief goes back to fix them. Building the rules in means they go in from the start and shape the schedule, so the review at the end is a check, not a repair job.

2. How Many Rules It Can Handle at Once

Residency scheduling involves dozens of simultaneous rules: rotation blocks that must be completed in sequence, call schedules that must be equitable, clinic assignments that can't overlap with certain rotations, conference leave, vacation requests, and subspecialty-specific rules that differ between programs. Ask whether the tool can model all of these, and what happens when rules conflict. Does it resolve them automatically, or does it surface a list of errors for the administrator to untangle?

3. Administrative Burden on Chief Residents

This is where the fit between a self-service tool and a GME program gets tested. A chief resident typically has a year in the role, competing clinical and educational responsibilities, and no formal training in the software they're expected to master. A platform that needs significant setup and ongoing configuration moves the work to whoever runs it. The question to ask is: does this tool require the chief to become a scheduling expert, or does it remove that requirement entirely?

The 5 Options for Physician and APP Scheduling in Residency Programs

1. Scheduling Wizard

Type: Managed Scheduling Service (Done-for-You)
Best For: Residency and fellowship programs that want the administrative burden of scheduling off their plate, with the ACGME rules built in

Scheduling Wizard is a managed service rather than software: a team does the build.

Programs submit their rules (rotations, residents, duty hour rules, preferences, subspecialty requirements) and our team delivers a complete, finished schedule: Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending, built to the ACGME requirements you tell us apply and to your fairness and coverage rules, delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you.

The YC-backed (W26) service currently serves 20+ hospitals and practices and 30+ departments.

Key Advantages:

  • Requirements built in: We don't flag violations after the fact; the rules go in while the schedule is built.
  • Zero software learning curve: There is no platform to learn, configure, or maintain. Chief residents submit rules and receive a finished schedule.
  • Institutional continuity across chief rotations: The program's written rule set lives with Scheduling Wizard, not in a spreadsheet that a graduating chief takes with them. New chiefs inherit the written rule set and last year's schedule, not a blank file.
  • Works alongside existing tools: it is entirely up to the department. Many keep the platform they already have for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules into it; others use our live view, or both.
  • Handles all schedule types: Block/rotation, call, clinic, and attending schedules, built together so they do not conflict, with resident preferences included.

The managed service model is particularly well-suited for programs where scheduling responsibility falls on a rotating chief rather than a dedicated, permanent administrator. It also keeps the program's rules written down when the chief changes.

What you get: the finished schedule as an Excel or Google Sheets file, and a custom live view if the department wants one. Major redrafts through the year are part of the engagement; day-to-day swaps stay with your team. For the specifics, see our page on healthcare staff scheduling software. We build to your rules and requests, however granular, with the ACGME requirements among them.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Ranked second because it is what many programs actually use. Every tool below is competing with a spreadsheet rather than with the others. It is free, everyone can open it, and it will hold any rule you can describe, including the ones that exist only as local custom.

On the three criteria above it scores poorly, and there is no pretending otherwise. Compliance automation: none. Rules handled at once: as many as a person can hold in their head, which is fewer than the schedule needs. Administrative burden on chief residents: the highest of anything here, because every hour of the work is theirs and none of it carries over to the next chief.

3. QGenda

Type: Self-Service Software (Enterprise)
Best For: Large academic medical centers with dedicated administrative staff and system-wide scheduling needs

QGenda is a workforce management platform used across health systems, built to handle scheduling at scale rather than for a single residency program.

For GME specifically, QGenda can track duty hours and flag potential ACGME violations. Resolving what it flags, and keeping the rules current, is the job of whoever runs the platform.

The bigger challenge for residency programs is the operational overhead. QGenda takes time to learn, set up and manage. That's manageable when a dedicated, non-rotating administrator owns the platform. It's much harder when the person responsible for scheduling changes every year. Programs that use QGenda successfully typically have a program coordinator or GME administrator who maintains continuity, not the chief resident.

Programs that already run QGenda can keep it and upload our finished schedules into it for day-to-day access.

4. Amion

Type: Publishing Platform
Best For: Publishing, sharing, and accessing completed schedules; widely used as a department-level communication tool

Amion is a familiar name in medicine, and it does its job well. That job is publishing schedules; building them is separate work.

In a typical Amion workflow, the chief builds the schedule with another tool or method, checks it against the ACGME requirements, and then puts it into Amion for the department. The build itself stays with the chief.

So Amion usually sits downstream, as the place the schedule is published. Paired with a managed service like Scheduling Wizard, it works well: Scheduling Wizard builds the schedule; the chief uploads the Excel output to Amion for department-wide visibility.

5. Lightning Bolt by PerfectServe

Type: Self-Service Software with Rules-Based Automation
Best For: Departments with complex, variable call patterns and an administrator willing to invest in deep platform configuration

Lightning Bolt generates schedules from user-defined rules. It's one of the more powerful self-service options available, particularly for departments where call patterns are highly variable and rule complexity is high.

The trade-off is setup investment. Lightning Bolt requires the user to define and input all scheduling rules within the platform's rule configuration, a process that requires both platform expertise and deep knowledge of your program's specific rules. Once configured well, it can automate significant portions of schedule generation. But that initial build, and the ongoing expertise required to maintain and update it, still lands on whoever is managing the platform. For a rotating chief resident, that's a steep ask.

The Decision Framework: Managed Service or Self-Service Software?

The most useful way to choose is to look at who in your program will actually do the scheduling.

Choose a self-service platform if:

  • You have a dedicated, non-rotating program coordinator or GME administrator with protected time to own the tool
  • That person has the technical aptitude and institutional continuity to configure and maintain complex scheduling rules year over year
  • You need system-wide scheduling visibility beyond a single residency program

Choose a managed service like Scheduling Wizard if:

  • Scheduling responsibility falls primarily on a rotating chief resident with competing clinical duties
  • Your program has experienced duty hour violations or scheduling inequities that manual processes failed to catch
  • Institutional scheduling knowledge is currently tied to individuals rather than a system, meaning it leaves with every graduating class
  • You want the ACGME requirements built in from the start, not checked at the end

There is evidence for building to written rules. A study published in Neurosurgery found that a rebuilt call schedule reduced call variation by 70%, a real gain in equity for the residents involved.

Which Option Fits a Residency Program

If your program runs on Excel templates rebuilt every year by a new chief resident, the question is who should be doing the build.

Self-service scheduling platforms, including good ones, need someone to learn them, maintain them and hand them off to the next chief. The institutional knowledge gap, the compliance risk, and the hours lost to manual scheduling recur every single year.

The tools in this list offer a range of approaches. For programs with dedicated administrative infrastructure, certain self-service platforms may be the right fit. For publishing and sharing completed schedules, Amion is a familiar choice. But for residency programs where the chief resident bears the scheduling burden (and where ACGME compliance, call equity, and continuity across annual transitions are non-negotiable) a managed service purpose-built for GME is the most direct path to solving the actual problem.

The aim is to give your chief residents back the time for clinical leadership.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between residency scheduling and general staff scheduling?

Residency scheduling involves satisfying complex, layered rules like ACGME rules, rotation sequences, and clinic requirements simultaneously, whereas general staff scheduling primarily focuses on filling open shifts with available personnel. General tools are built for coverage; residency scheduling tools must be built for compliance, fairness, and educational requirements, making it a different and more complex problem to solve.

How can our residency program keep its schedule inside the ACGME rules?

The most effective way to keep a schedule inside the ACGME rules is to have the rules go into the build directly, so they shape the schedule from the start. Then the review at the end is a check rather than a round of corrections for the chief resident.

Do we have to give up existing tools like Amion to use Scheduling Wizard?

No. It is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way, and deliver it in the format and structure you want: Excel or Google Sheets, or a custom live view we build for you if that is useful. Many programs keep Amion for day-to-day viewing and upload our schedules straight into it; others use the live view, or both. Whatever works best for your program.

How do scheduling tools handle subspecialty-specific ACGME requirements?

With a managed service, you tell us which subspecialty requirements apply (for Surgery, Anesthesiology, Internal Medicine and so on) and they are written down with your own rules before the first build. When evaluating platforms, it's critical to ask whether they can model your specific rules or if you are responsible for manually inputting and maintaining them, as this can be a significant source of error and administrative work.

What is the main advantage of a managed scheduling service over self-service software for a chief resident?

The main advantage is that the administrative burden goes to the service and the institutional knowledge stays written down. A managed service removes the need for the chief resident to learn software, configure rules, and manually build schedules. It also solves the knowledge transfer problem that occurs when a graduating chief takes their scheduling expertise with them, ensuring continuity and stability for the program year after year.
